notes.meaning: The Lord sends Moses back to Pharaoh with the same royal demand: release Israel so they can worship Him. God calls Himself 'the God of the Hebrews,' showing that He personally defends His oppressed people. Israel belongs to God, not to the king of Egypt.
God warns Pharaoh what will happen if he keeps holding the people back. Giving this warning beforehand shows God's patience and gives the king another chance to turn from his stubborn ways.

A deadly sickness is threatened against Egyptian livestock out in the open fields. This judgment falls directly from God's hand without Aaron using his staff. Because Egypt had made God's people poor through slavery, God now strikes Egypt's wealth.

The Lord promises to protect the animals belonging to Israel so that none of them die. This clear separation proved that the sickness was not a random accident, but guided by the living God. God watches over and guards what belongs to His own people.

God sets an exact time by announcing that the plague will happen tomorrow. By naming the day in advance, the Lord proved that the event was completely under His control. It also gave the Egyptians time to think and turn back before the blow fell.

The next day, the disease struck the Egyptian herds in the fields, while not a single animal of the Israelites died. The word 'all' means that huge numbers across the land were destroyed, though some animals kept indoors survived. This also dealt a heavy blow to Egyptian religion, which treated cattle as sacred gods.

Pharaoh sent messengers to check on Goshen and found that not one Israelite animal had died. Even with clear proof of God's protection, Pharaoh remained stubborn and refused to let the people go. He closed his mind against the truth because his heart was weighed down by pride.

God commands Moses and Aaron to take handfuls of furnace ashes and toss them into the air in front of Pharaoh. The furnace was a reminder of the cruel brick-making labor Egypt forced upon Israel. Now, the soot from those oppressive kilns becomes the very tool of Egypt's punishment.

The scattered soot turns into fine dust across Egypt and causes painful, blistering sores on people and animals. This sixth plague arrived without any advance warning. For the first time, human bodies were directly attacked, showing that worse judgments would come if Pharaoh refused to yield.

Moses obeyed God and threw the ashes toward heaven right in Pharaoh's presence. At once, burning sores broke out on people and animals across the land. God showed that even the air itself must obey His command to carry out His justice.

Pharaoh's royal magicians were so covered with painful boils that they could not even stand before Moses. Their secret arts could not protect their own bodies, let alone cure anyone else. They were publicly put to shame and forced to abandon their contest against God.

Pharaoh still refused to listen, but now the text states that the Lord hardened his heart. Because Pharaoh had repeatedly shut his eyes and hardened himself against God's previous warnings, God gave him over to his own stubborn rebellion. Refusing God's mercy again and again leaves a person numb to the truth.

differ.view: God's hardening is judicial, withdrawing His restraining grace only after a person repeatedly refuses to repent by their own free will.

notes.meaning: God tells Moses to confront Pharaoh early in the morning with the exact same demand to let His people go. Repeating the command showed that God does not change His mind or lower His standard. God patiently repeats His truth even to a rebellious ruler.

The Lord warns that the coming plagues will strike at Pharaoh's very heart and shake his court. The earlier plagues brought discomfort and loss of property, but now the blows will cut to his inner core. These heavy judgments would prove that the God of Israel has no equal anywhere on earth.

God explains that He could easily have wiped Pharaoh and his people off the earth in a single moment with disease. The king's survival was not due to his own strength, but to God's restraint. God held back His full power to give space for His greater purpose to unfold.

God kept Pharaoh alive on the throne so that His supreme power might be displayed through him. The ruler's stubborn defiance became the stage where God's mighty acts were demonstrated for all generations to see. As a result, the fame of the Lord's name would travel to every nation.

differ.view: God raised up and appointed Pharaoh from eternity as an instrument of wrath to make His power known in Pharaoh's destruction.
God preserved Pharaoh alive through past plagues instead of cutting him off, turning his self-chosen stubbornness into an occasion to reveal divine power.

notes.meaning: The Lord challenges Pharaoh for still setting himself up as a high barrier against Israel's freedom. The king acted like a rampart blocking God's people from marching out. Resisting God's people is the same as fighting against God Himself.

God promises that by this same time tomorrow, He will send the most destructive hailstorm in Egypt's entire history. Rain and violent storms were rare in Egypt, making such weather abnormal and terrifying. God gave an exact advance notice so everyone would know the storm was sent by Him.

God mercifully warns Pharaoh and his people to bring their workers and surviving animals under cover before the storm hits. Anyone left outside in the open fields will be struck down and killed by the heavy hail. Even while announcing severe judgment, God provides a way of escape for those who listen.

Egyptian officials who took God's warning seriously rushed their servants and cattle indoors, while those who scoffed left everything in the fields. Some of Pharaoh's own officers had finally learned to fear the Lord's word after seeing the previous plagues. Those who ignored the warning brought ruin upon themselves through careless unbelief.

The Lord commands Moses to stretch his hand toward the sky so the hail can fall across Egypt. Stretching toward heaven showed that this disaster came directly from God above, where Egyptian gods had no power. The storm was sent to strike people, animals, and crops alike.

When Moses held out his staff toward heaven, the Lord sent rolling thunder, crushing hail, and lightning that ran along the ground. Fire and ice fell together, showing that nature's opposing elements were united in obeying their Maker. The sight was terrifying and unlike any ordinary weather.

Hail poured down with continuous flashes of fire flashing through it. The storm was far more terrible than anything Egypt had ever experienced since it became a nation. God showed that all creation answers to His voice and carries out His word.

The massive hailstones killed every person and animal left out in the open. It smashed the crops in the fields and stripped the branches off the trees. Those who ignored God's gracious warning suffered the full loss He had foretold.

The land of Goshen was completely spared, with no hail falling where the Israelites lived. This dramatic protection right beside the ruined Egyptian fields proved God's special care for His people. The Lord guards those who belong to Him even when judgment falls all around them.

In sheer panic, Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron and confessed that he had sinned. He acknowledged that the Lord is righteous and that he and his people were guilty. His words sounded right, but his confession came from terror over the storm rather than true sorrow for offending God.

Pharaoh begged Moses to pray for the thunder and hail to stop, promising that he would finally let Israel leave. The king could not bear the terrifying sound of God's thunder any longer. Under the pressure of trouble, people often make promises to God that they quickly forget once relief comes.

Moses agreed to go outside the city walls and spread out his hands in prayer so the storm would stop. This miracle would prove to Pharaoh that the entire earth belongs to the Lord, not to Pharaoh or Egyptian gods. Stepping out into the deadly storm showed Moses' complete confidence in God's protection.

Moses frankly told Pharaoh that neither he nor his officials truly feared the Lord God yet. Moses saw through the king's smooth words, knowing that fear of punishment is not the same as genuine reverence. True faith shows itself in willing obedience, not in brief panic.

The flax and barley were completely ruined because the barley had already formed heads and the flax was in bud. The wheat and spelt were spared because they ripened later and were still tender beneath the soil. Even in devastating judgment, God left a portion of the harvest to give Egypt another opportunity to turn to Him.

Moses walked outside the city and lifted his hands in prayer to the Lord. Instantly, the thunder, hail, and torrential rain ceased falling. God heard His servant's prayer and showed His complete mastery over the skies.

As soon as Pharaoh saw that the storm had passed and the danger was gone, he went back on his word and hardened his heart. His officials followed his lead in rebelling against the Lord. Turning back to sin after receiving mercy only adds to a person's guilt.

Pharaoh's heart remained hard, and he refused to let the people of Israel go. Everything happened exactly as the Lord had predicted through Moses. Human stubbornness never derails God's plans; it only fulfills what He has already foretold.
